newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-High-flying NZ dollar could lose its wings.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-High-flying NZ dollar could lose its wings.

text.p: By Robin Clements, economist at SBC Warburg.
WELLINGTON, Oct 4 - It is often the case that when a consensus forms about some economic or market development, that is the very time to be contrary and take an opposing view.

Such a situation has developed in the currency market where local economists, investors, exporters, politicians and, we would argue, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, agree that the New Zealand dollar is higher than need be and is likely to fall.
Trouble is, as has been the case for the last four years, this simply has not happened -- instead, the Trade-Weighted Index recently hit an 8-year high.

With overnight cash and short term bank bill rates over 9.9 percent and the 1-year bond yield around 8.75 percent, there is no need to look further for an answer as to why investors find New Zealand dollars attractive.
However, prevailing interest rate differentials versus other countries are not the only factor which influence a currency's performance.
So, of the factors that do matter the most, what -- ultimately -- could cause an adjustment in the currency?
For ease of exposition, we group the various influences into three areas:

* Interest Rate Differentials: This covers both short and long term rates (usually expressed in real -- after inflation -- terms). The Eurobond/Samurai market is currently attracted to yields on the shorter dated bonds.

* Capital Flows: This is a catch-all item, which covers such diverse topics as confidence in government policies (i.e. the quality of decisions), the openness of capital markets (e.g. financial/goods market regulation), through to corporate performance and direct investment opportunities.

* Economic Fundamentals: As opposed to the two short term influences above, this area tends to be of longer term consideration. Issues of relevance are relative inflation and external trade performance, where the terms of trade (dominated by commodity prices) are an important element of the latter.
Clearly, these three areas are interrelated and it is impossible to isolate -- in any particular instance -- exactly what the contribution of each is.

In particular, New Zealand's monetary policy framework -- with its sole price stability objective -- makes the New Zealand currency market somewhat unique in that it is monetary policy that drives several of the factors above.

In other words, tight monetary policy holds interest rates up, while low inflation is a discipline on fiscal profligacy -- thus high rates, responsible government and low inflation credibility all add up to a strong currency.
What could undermine the New Zealand dollar?
We have approached this question by considering what could constitute threats to the currency at various points over the next year or so.
(Note: when reference is made to the NZD/currency, we are meaning the average level of the currency, i.e. the Trade-Weighted Index.)
* Pre-Election (12 October).
Current monetary policy considerations will keep short rates high, while Eurokiwi/Samurai issues continue to buoy sentiment.
However:
(1) upside is capped by the RBNZ -- the Bank is unlikely to respond to a TWI under 67 but could to a spike much over 67 (possibly accompanied by a tolerance for lower short rates), and;
(2) political concerns intensifying as the election approaches i.e. the risk of lower short rates, loss of confidence, higher inflation.
Bottom line: if there is upside, it is limited by the RBNZ, whereas there is far greater risk of downside -- in a short period of time.
* Post-Election/Pre-Government (14 October - 13 December at latest)
This is from election night through to the announcement of a new MMP government. In this case, current monetary policy arrangements remain in force and the scenarios are:
- Centre-Right: National-Led Coalition
Currency rises on relief rally (confidence boost) -- if election outcome looks decisive, this could be immediate and sharp (with a perception that the strength could be sustained).
However, like the pre-elction period, there is still the cap applied by the RBNZ, since there would be no change in the framework.
- Centre-Left: labour-Led Coalition

Mixed implications -- widening of inflation target band to -1.0 to 3.0 percent but greater government spending. We think the bias would be to the downside (but within RBNZ "comfort bands") -- talk of more "realistic" exchange rate, loss of confidence and higher inflation expectations from the wider inflation target band.
- Left-of-Centre Coalition

Again, if the election night result looks decisive, the market response could be swift -- on the downside. In the first instance, the RBNZ would be bound to defend the currency (above 64) by raising short rates -- possibly dramatically.
However, this may be insufficient to stem the loss of confidence and perceived risk of higher inflation.
Botttom line -- only the centre-right outcome would see a rise and, even then, this could be transitory -- being limited by the RBNZ. Whereas the risk on the downside is of far greater magnitude.
* MMP Government/Monetary Policy
This is when the deals have been done, the coalitions formed and the new MMP government announced and policy details are emerging. Again we consider the various scenarios:
- Centre-Right: National-Led Coalition
Comments on currency spike and RBNZ cap still apply. Any easing will be dependent upon inflation prospects/real economy indicators.

Largely status quo policy, uncertainty as regards the policy framework and government spending no longer relevant but higher wage inflation risks (June quarter Quarterly Employment Survey data) -- on balance, still on track for easing by the end of
199,6 maybe early 1997, i.e. short rates fall.
- Centre-Left: Labour-Led Coalition

Wider -1.0 to 3.0 percent inflation band implemented (change to RBNZ Governor's Policy Target Agreement) and increased spending plans confirmed. Initial expectation is that the wider band will allow the RBNZ to ease earlier (current inflation under the 3 percent top end) but equally, it will take a threat to -1.0 percent (i.e. not zero) to trigger an easing, while increased spending will pose upside demand/inflation risks.
On balance, we think the overall impact will be negative for the currency -- reflecting the impact of lower confidence/higher inflation expectations.
- Left-of-Centre Coalition

If the RBNZ is given multiple targets (via a Section 12 override) and (RBNZ governor) Dr Brash resigns, then the currency direction is clear cut! On the other hand, if the changes are more moderate (e.g. Labour's wider band), then the lack of adjustment (lower interest rates, exchange rates) could lead to further policy change i.e. the intent of the policy change is to achieve easier conditions.
Either way, lower short rates, a loss of confidence and higher inflation will produce currency weakness.

Bottom line -- even the best of outcomes leads to a lower currency, albeit perhaps a little later than would otherwise be the case if policies shift to favour higher government spending and a tolerance for higher inflation.
* Other Possible Adjustment Mechanisms
1) Recession -- not likely unless confidence plummets;

2) Higher short rates offshore -- probable but only in time. We see the Fed tightening by 50 basis points before year-end but it will be the second quarter of 1997 before Japan and Germany are in tightening mode.
3) Balance of Payments deterioration -- possible but not expected and it would take several quarters before it became a market concern.
4) Collapse in the terms of trade -- unlikely given global growth prospects -- we see the risks still to the upside.
Conclusions:
The two factors which will have the greatest bearing on New Zealand currency prospects in the near term will be:
1) Politics, and; 2) the real economy.

It seems to us that the only scenario that sees sustained currency strength is a National-led majority with status quo policies (we rate a 55:45 chance) and a real economy that fails to buckle under the weight of high interest rates/currency (we think it is slowing).

Bottom line -- Under most likely scenarios, the upside potential for the currency is limited. Moreover, if the currency clears the first hurdle (political), it will immediately face up to the next (monetary policy easing).
With the TWI around 66.5, we favour the downside.
(Note - The views expressed in the above article are those of the author and are not attributable to Reuters.)
